analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government plan covering everyone, with no premiums or copays.
analysis.headline: The Medicare for All Act had 15 Senate supporters — one Independent sponsor and 14 Democratic cosponsors — but never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace today's mix of private insurance, employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and the ACA exchanges with a single national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services. Every U.S. resident would be enrolled automatically and covered for hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health treatment, dental, vision, long-term care, reproductive care, and more, with no deductibles or copays (a small annual charge for prescriptions is allowed). Private insurers could only sell extra coverage on top of the government plan, not the basic coverage they sell today. The bill was introduced in May 2023, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never brought up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain health coverage with no premiums, deductibles, or copays for covered care — the roughly 26 million uninsured, people who skip care because of cost, and anyone paying high out-of-pocket bills for drugs, dental, vision, mental health, or long-term care. Hospitals and doctors would get one payment system instead of billing hundreds of insurers. Employers would no longer pay most workers' health premiums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone needing health care, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident would be entitled to coverage, enrolled automatically at birth or upon establishing residency, replacing the patchwork of private plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and ACA exchanges.

The bill bans deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments for covered services — the only allowed patient charge is a prescription drug cost-sharing schedule capped at $200 a year, waived entirely for people below 250% of the poverty line.

Coverage would be comprehensive, including hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance use treatment, dental, vision, and hearing, home- and community-based long-term care, reproductive care including abortion, and gender-affirming care — benefits many current plans exclude or charge heavily for.
Private insurers and employers could only offer coverage that supplements, not duplicates, the government plan, ending the private market for basic health insurance.
The government would negotiate prescription drug prices and set a national formulary, and hospitals would be paid through fixed annual global budgets rather than per-service billing.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the program through new taxes; the bill creates a Medicare for All Trust Fund but leaves the specific tax changes to separate legislation. Workers in insurance administration and medical billing would lose jobs (the bill sets aside 1% of the health budget for up to 5 years of wage replacement and retraining for them). Hospitals and drug makers would face government-set payment rates and drug prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, insurers, drug makers, billing workers

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a trust fund and payment system but does not specify the taxes that would pay for it; moving from today's mix of employer premiums, payroll taxes, and state spending to a single federal tax would mean large tax increases for many households and businesses, even if most people's total health spending fell.

The transition would disrupt jobs and industries: private insurers would lose their core business (limited to supplemental coverage), and health insurance administration and billing workers would face dislocation — the bill budgets only up to 5 years of temporary assistance for them.

A single government payer setting hospital global budgets and a national drug formulary concentrates enormous power in HHS; critics argue government budgeting can lead to wait times or underpayment, while supporters point to other countries running similar systems. The bill's own text acknowledges the risk by requiring regional reviews and reserve funds for unanticipated costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the trade is straightforward: whatever they pay in premiums, deductibles, and copays today would be replaced by some share of a new tax, and the bill eliminates out-of-pocket charges entirely for covered care. The honest costs are the tax increase, the loss of about 500,000+ insurance and billing jobs with only temporary help, and the risk that one government payer sets prices too low or budgets too tight. The bill includes real guardrails (regional budget reviews, reserve funds, appeals, an ombudsman) but its financing is left unwritten, so the net effect on any given family depends on tax details this bill never supplied.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2023, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 17, 2023, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded: the Finance Committee held no markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor during the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, drug makers, and everyone employed in the private insurance and medical-billing systems are better off because the bill died — the health coverage status quo, with employer premiums, deductibles, and private insurers as gatekeepers, continues unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, drug makers, and the billing industry

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare for All Act and recruited 14 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 14 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Baldwin, Blumenthal, Booker, Gillibrand, Heinrich, Hirono, Luján, Markey, Merkley, Padilla, Schatz, Warren, Welch, Whitehouse)

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; the committee recorded no action after the referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 Senate supporters were Democrats plus Independent sponsor Sanders; not a single Republican cosponsored, and the bill's fate was decided in a committee chaired by a Democrat who never brought it up.

industries.note: The bill outlaws selling health insurance that duplicates the government plan, restricting insurers to selling extra benefits on top of it — eliminating their core market. Insurers profit today by collecting premiums and limiting payouts, so their interest runs against a plan that covers everyone with no cost-sharing.

HHS would negotiate drug prices and set a national formulary for the entire population, replacing today's fragmented negotiating where manufacturers set prices against many insurers. Drug makers' revenue depends on high U.S. prices, so their interest runs against consumers here.

Hospitals would be paid through fixed quarterly global budgets instead of billing per service — ending billing and collection costs and bad debt, but capping revenue and subjecting budgets to government negotiation. Patients lose nothing directly; the tradeoff is between hospital revenue and taxpayer cost.

industries.industry: Health insurance administration and medical billing
industries.note: With one payer and no per-service billing for hospitals, much of the claims-processing and billing workforce would be unneeded; the bill funds only up to 5 years of wage replacement and retraining at 1% of the health budget. Their interest is in keeping the current fragmented system.

Employers would stop paying most workers' health premiums, a major cost, but would be barred from providing coverage duplicating the government plan. Workers gain coverage; employers gain cost relief — their interests align in this bill.
